transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-29
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Cho (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (CTO, Prism), Maya Singh (ML Eng), Oliver Wu (Infra)

Summary (auto):
Initial discovery focused on latency/throughput requirements for a payments fraud detection assistant. Customer looking at Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; key questions around p95 latency targets for streaming responses, concurrency (simultaneous sessions), and token/sec benchmarking for short bursty requests (8-64 tokens) vs longer generation (200-800 tokens). Security and SOC2/SSO requirements discussed briefly. Next: share benchmarks, pricing, schedule POC scoping.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:05] Raj: yep, loud and clear, thanks Sofia.
[00:08] Sofia: great, this is Sofia from Redwood, AE on the account, Ethan our solutions engineer is here as well, quick round-robin?
[00:15] Raj: Raj, CTO at Prism, we're focused on productionizing an LLM for fraud detection assistance.
[00:18] Maya: Maya, ML eng, working on model integration and evaluation.
[00:21] Oliver: Oliver, infra - networking and security owner.
[00:24] Ethan: Ethan, Redwood SE, I'll cover benchmarks and architecture.

[00:30] Sofia: cool, high-level - are you evaluating hosted API first or already looking at Dedicated/Private?
[00:38] Raj: ideally we want to start Hosted for speed but switch to Dedicated or Private if latency and data controls require it. Our p95 targets are strict though - sub 200ms for short answers and sub 800ms for streaming longer responses at p95.
[00:52] Maya: right, our user flows are chatty - lots of short queries (8-32 tokens) and occasional longer explainers up to 600 tokens. We also need streaming for UI so initial token latency is important.

[01:10] Ethan: ok that's helpful. For Hosted we usually publish p95 numbers for standard models - but important to note that p95 is sensitive to concurrency and request size. Can you share your expected concurrency?
[01:22] Raj: our goal is 1,200 concurrent sessions peak, but most sessions are low activity, maybe 300 sustained. Also bursty spikes during payroll windows - brief 3-5 minute spikes where concurrency jumps 3-5x.
[01:37] Oliver: also want to know how streaming affects bandwidth and token/sec billing; we run in multiple regions and want predictable cost.

[01:46] Ethan: makes sense. Roughly for similar customers: Hosted p95 for short requests (<=32 tokens) on a 1-caller-per-request baseline is around 80-180ms depending on model and region; Dedicated lowers variance and can hit consistent sub-100ms p95 if you reserve capacity and tune batching and KV caching. For long streaming (>200 tokens) p95 depends on token generation speed - we often quote token/sec numbers per model (e.g., 60-120 tokens/sec on optimized kernels on A100-class GPUs, higher on L40/Hopper).
[02:16] Maya: token/sec 60-120 - that's broad, how do you measure that? what's the test harness?
[02:21] Ethan: we measure modeled token/sec under continuous generation with batching disabled to simulate single-stream throughput, and we do a separate bench with continuous batching to show aggregate throughput. We'll share the CSV of recent runs - it includes prompt length distribution, beam/temperature settings, tokenizer artifacts.

[02:42] Raj: question - p95 targets we care about are for first-byte and tail during streaming; do you split those metrics?
[02:48] Ethan: yes we report initial response latency (time-to-first-byte) plus per-token generation delta. For streaming, network path matters - we instrument regional POPs. For Private deployments you can run inference on-prem with a control plane in your VPC which reduces network variance.

[03:06] Oliver: if we go Dedicated, what's autoscaling behavior - will we see consistent p95 under spikes?
[03:11] Sofia: Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools with configurable autoscaling and burst capacity. For spikes we recommend a small reserved commit sized for sustained load and a burst pool for short term; that prevents cold-start variance and keeps p95 stable.
[03:25] Ethan: also prefix/KV cache reduces repeated prompt costs and lowers tail latency - especially for session-based assistants. If you have repeated context or system prompts, caching cuts the per-request compute.

[03:38] Maya: about KV cache - many docs call it KV cache but sometimes auto transcribe as "KV cash" (laughs), just making sure we understand: is that in-memory on the GPU or external?
[03:47] Ethan: the KV cache (on-device) is kept on the GPU for active sessions; we also have a fast shared cache layer for prefix reuse. For Private on-prem you can control cache eviction policies.

[03:59] Raj: security - we require SOC 2 and enterprise SSO/SAML, and KMS integration for key management. Any red flags for Hosted?
[04:07] Sofia: Hosted supports SOC 2, bring-your-own-key via KMS in some plans, and SSO/SAML for console access. For sensitive data and audit requirements customers choose Dedicated or Private for full control and audit logs.

[04:20] Oliver: audit logs - are per-token traces stored? we need to ensure retention policies and PII redaction.
[04:26] Ethan: we can configure logging level - you can capture request/response hashes and metadata and keep actual content out or stored encrypted. We'll share the security checklist.

[04:36] Maya: ok, technical - can you give example p95 numbers at different concurrencies?
[04:40] Ethan: sure, rough numbers from internal benchmarks for a mid-sized decoder model:
- single-req short (<=32 tokens): p95 ~ 90ms at low concurrency, ~140ms at 500 concurrent, ~220ms at 2k concurrent on shared hosted.
- Dedicated with reserved GPUs: p95 ~ 70-100ms even at 1k concurrent if provisioned correctly.
- streaming initial TTFB: usually 60-120ms depending on region and model; thereafter tokens/sec 50-110 tokens/sec per stream on typical GPUs.

[05:15] Raj: those hosted numbers suggest at 1.2k peak we might see p95 ~200ms which is borderline. Could we shard across regions or models?
[05:22] Ethan: yes - smart routing can send traffic to lower-latency regions or cheaper model variants; you can also pin to model quantization profiles which drop token/sec but save cost. We can do an A/B: small quantized variant for non-critical flows, full precision for high-value flows.

[05:38] Maya: on quantization - we worry about quality regressions. Do you provide eval tooling to monitor generation quality per rollout?
[05:44] Sofia: Redwood Optimize has eval hooks and regression alerts tied to prompt sets; you can set prompt collections and get quality metrics after model or quantization changes.

[05:55] Oliver: network: we run in GCP us-central and AWS eu-west; can Redwood support multi-cloud region routing?
[06:01] Ethan: yes, we route by region and you can set policies. Private deployment can be placed in your VPC. For Dedicated, we have options in major cloud regions.

[06:12] Raj: can you run an on-site benchmark with our prompts? we want token/sec and p95 across a 2-hour simulated traffic window including spikes.
[06:18] Ethan: absolutely - typical POC uses your prompt set. We'll run both Hosted and Dedicated bench runs: steady-state and spike window, and provide raw CSV with latencies per request and tokens/sec.

[06:30] Maya: what about concurrent streaming sessions - how do you measure aggregate throughput? If we have 1k concurrent streams each generating 5 tokens/sec that's a lot.
[06:37] Ethan: aggregate throughput scales with batchable work; continuous streaming is less batchable but we rely on kernel-level optimizations and multi-stream scheduling. We'll provide recommended instance types and estimated tokens/sec aggregate. For example, a 4-GPU Dedicated pool with optimized kernels can sustain tens of thousands of tokens/sec aggregate.

[06:58] Raj: pricing - does token/sec affect billing or is billing strictly tokens?
[07:03] Sofia: billing is token-based for Hosted (input+output tokens) and for Dedicated it's a combination of reserved capacity + overage token pricing. Token/sec isn't billed directly but it influences capacity sizing which affects cost.

[07:16] Oliver: any pitfalls - like cold starts or batch buildup causing tail spikes?
[07:20] Ethan: cold starts are rare if you reserve capacity; batch buildup can increase latency when request rates are low and the runtime waits to form larger batches, but we use dynamic batching thresholds and latency SLOs to avoid that. We can tune batch timers to favor latency over throughput for your real-time flows.

[07:38] Maya: what telemetry do we get? we want per-route p95, token counts, KV cache hit rates, model variant rollouts.
[07:44] Sofia: Redwood Console provides per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, KV cache hit rates, tracing, and alerting. You can also export metrics to your monitoring stack.

[07:55] Raj: ok this is helpful. Can you summarize concrete steps for the POC?
[07:59] Ethan: we'll need your prompt set and a traffic profile (concurrency over time). We'll run: Hosted bench (3 runs), Dedicated bench with reserved commit sizing (3 runs), and a Private deployment estimate if you want on-prem numbers. We'll return CSVs, recommended commit size, and a latency/cost comparison sheet.

[08:19] Raj: timeline - can you run that next week?
[08:21] Ethan: yes - if we get the prompts and traffic profile by Friday, we can run benches early next week and have results by Wednesday.

[08:29] Maya: small note - we have HIPAA-adjacent data, need to confirm data residency and encryption in transit and at rest.
[08:36] Sofia: we'll include security docs and highlight what Hosted vs Dedicated provides; Private can be set for stricter residency and KMS control.

[08:45] Oliver: one more - integration with our SSO and SCIM for user provisioning.
[08:49] Ethan: supported - we'll provide the SAML/SCIM integration guide.

[08:55] Sofia: alright, recap of next steps: Sofia sends pricing and Dedicated vs Hosted writeup; Ethan shares benchmark harness and recent CSVs; customer to provide prompt set and traffic profile; schedule POC scoping next week.

[09:10] Raj: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[09:12] Maya: thanks.
[09:13] Oliver: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
